draft_body:
My holidays used to have client meetings in them. Now I say no.

Right now I probably can't take on another client, either.
That's a sacrifice I'm willing to make.

Back then I was at a consulting firm in New York,
at the whims of my employer and of my clients.
Meetings got booked last minute, in time zones I didn't choose.

We'd been in New York six years when our first kid was born.

We moved home to Australia, and I hadn't figured out what came next.
I got to be home for a long stretch after she was born.
I felt lucky to have that.

Going out on my own had been in the back of my mind for a while.
Moving home forced it. I did it straight away.

My hard stop is four o'clock on the days I pick up my daughter.
Her community kinder shuts at four, and my wife and I coordinate pickup.

Other days, the laptop typically closes around five.
It stays closed until the kids are in bed,
then I open it again to finish a few things.

It changed how I work for myself, too.

I need to be careful with my time, so I track it.
I put an ops system in place that shows what it goes towards:
utilisation per client against my goals, and my effective hourly rate.

Then it's about making trade-offs.

I recently told a client I couldn't make some of their meetings because of pickup.
I was comfortable saying so, because our values line up.
And no, I'm not taking the piss with it.

It means I get to spend more time with the kids.
verdict:
And no, I'm not taking the piss with it.

It's how I've intentionally structured things.

draft_body:
SDR leaders: I worked out the SDR-to-AE ratio at 2,206 US software companies.

One company size breaks the pattern.

AEs here means new-business sellers. Account managers aren't counted.

AEs per SDR:

51 to 200 employees: 4.8
201 to 500: 4.7
501 to 1,000: 4.6
1,001 to 5,000: 6.2
5,001 to 10,000: 10.0
10,000+: 14.2

The line is 1,000 employees.

Below it, the ratio sits at about one SDR for every 4.7 AEs in every size band. If you're building an SDR team somewhere under 1,000 people, that's what your peers have.

If you're heading past 1,000, the companies already there carry fewer SDRs per AE, and the bigger they get, the fewer. By 10,000+ employees, it's a third of the coverage.

That holds with each band's 10 biggest teams taken out.

My bet is the pipeline changes. More demand comes in on its own, and AEs start prospecting their own named accounts.

I haven't tested it. And I only counted US profiles, so an SDR team based overseas wouldn't show up either.

If you've run SDRs at a company past 1,000 people, did inbound and your AEs pick up the slack?

SDR leaders: I worked out the SDR-to-AE ratio at 2,206 US software companies.

I've got a theory on why, past 1,000 employees, it stops holding.

AEs per SDR:

- 51-200 employees: 4.8
- 201-500: 4.7
- 501-1,000: 4.6
- 1,001-5,000: 6.2
- 5,001-10,000: 10.0
- 10,000+: 14.2

Below 1,000 employees, the ratio sits at about one SDR for every 4.7 AEs in every size band. If you're building an SDR team somewhere under 1,000 people, that's what your peers have.

If you're heading past 1,000, the companies already there carry fewer SDRs per AE, and the bigger they get, the fewer. By 10,000+ employees, it's a third of the coverage.

That holds with each band's 10 biggest teams taken out as well.

My bet is the pipeline changes. More demand comes in on its own, and AEs start prospecting their own named accounts.

I've increasingly seen companies push AEs towards sourcing their own deals, to get more out of the team they've already got. That's anecdotal, though.

And I only counted US profiles, so SDR teams based overseas wouldn't show up.

If you've run SDRs at a company past 1,000 people, did inbound and your AEs pick up the slack or something else?
